content: The phenomenon of male lactation in humans has become increasingly observed in recent years, primarily due to the use of medications that stimulate the mammary glands in men. While it is widely known that males have nipples, many are unaware that they also possess mammary glands. Typically, the amount of mammary tissue in males is minimal and not noticeable. However, when male breast tissue develops visibly, the condition is referred to as gynecomastia. Under the appropriate hormonal stimulation—similar to the hormonal changes that occur in females during pregnancy and childbirth—the mammary glands in males can produce milk. However, the volume of milk produced by males is significantly lower compared to that of lactating females. Interestingly, male lactation has, in some cases, occurred without the use of hormonal treatments. For example, newborn baby boys (and girls) can occasionally produce milk due to the intense hormonal exposure during their mother’s pregnancy and the hours surrounding childbirth. This phenomenon is known as witch’s milk. Male lactation is most commonly associated with hormonal treatments administered to men undergoing therapy for prostate cancer. In such cases, female hormones are used to slow the growth of cancerous prostate tissue, but these same hormones can also stimulate the mammary glands, leading to milk production. Additionally, male-to-female transgender individuals may experience lactation as a result of the hormones they take to feminize their bodies. Male lactation can also occur as a side effect of certain antipsychotic medications. Extreme stress, combined with demanding physical activity and insufficient food intake, has also been documented as a cause of male lactation. This phenomenon was first studied in survivors of Nazi concentration camps liberated after World War II. Similarly, some American prisoners of war returning from the Korean and Vietnam Wars experienced male lactation. It is also possible for males (and females) to induce lactation through consistent nipple stimulation, such as massage or simulated sucking, over an extended period of time, often lasting months. This mechanical stimulation can lead to the release of prolactin, a hormone that promotes milk production. Male lactation is not exclusive to humans and has been observed in certain non-human species. For instance, the Dayak fruit bat (Dyacopterus spadiceus) is known for lactating males, which may assist in nursing their offspring. Male goats have also been reported to lactate on occasion. Spontaneous male lactation and even nursing have been observed in rare cases in humans. Jared Diamond has reported instances of male and female cancer patients treated with estrogen who began lactating after being injected with prolactin. He also suggests that mechanical stimulation of male breasts, by releasing prolactin, could induce lactation. Furthermore, there are accounts of teenage boys lactating after self-stimulation of their nipples.
